goal: Compare sync/atomic vs sync.Mutex for hot counters, and evaluate atomic.Pointer[time.Time] for last-output timestamps in Go. Produce a recommendation per use case with tradeoffs and concrete code patterns.
background:
Two related Go concurrency design decisions:

1. Hot counters: a value (e.g. request counter, work-item counter, byte counter) incremented from many goroutines on every event. Candidates: sync/atomic (AddInt64/AddUint64/atomic.Int64/atomic.Uint64) vs sync.Mutex protecting a plain int64. Evaluate throughput under contention, correctness, memory-ordering semantics, race-detector behavior, code clarity, common pitfalls (e.g. alignment on 32-bit platforms before Go 1.19, mixing atomic and non-atomic access), and when one outperforms the other.

2. Last-output timestamps: a time.Time that gets overwritten when an event happens (e.g. last activity, last write, last heartbeat) and read by watchers/timeout checkers. Candidate: atomic.Pointer[time.Time] (Go 1.19+) vs sync.Mutex around a time.Time field vs storing time.Time as Unix nanoseconds in atomic.Int64. Evaluate correctness of pointer publication, allocation overhead per update, read-side cost, monotonicity considerations, and idiomatic Go patterns.

Evaluation dimensions: performance under contention, correctness (data races, torn reads, memory ordering), idiomatic Go (linters, race detector), code clarity, Go version compatibility, common bugs.

Deliverable: per-decision recommendation with short code patterns (5-15 lines each) showing the preferred approach, plus the conditions under which the other approach is better. Cite Go documentation, sync/atomic package docs, and well-known references where relevant.

This is a general Go design comparison; not tied to a specific source file in this repo.
